core.text: A dictionary lists a Latin verb by **the principal parts (the four dictionary forms that give a verb's present, perfect and participle stems)**: *pulsō, pulsāre, pulsāvī, pulsātum*. Everything the verb can do is built on three stems hidden in parts two to four. The infinitive gives the present stem (*pulsā-*), for present, imperfect and future. The third part gives the perfect stem (*pulsāv-*), for 'did / had done'. The fourth gives the participle stem (*pulsāt-*), for 'having been done' and the passive past. Latin name: *partēs prīncipālēs verbī*.
English verbs have parts too: *begin, began, begun*. *Began* makes the past, *begun* makes *has begun* and *was begun*.
Learn the three stems: present (infinitive minus -re), perfect (third part minus -ī), participle (fourth part minus -um).

invented.la: Mārcus scrībit; herī scrīpsit; epistula scrīpta est.
invented.en: Marcus writes; yesterday he wrote; the letter has been written.

core.text: The third part *is* the first person of **the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense)**: *pulsāvī* = I hit. So the dictionary entry already gives you one whole perfect form; the other endings replace its -ī.

teach.title: One verb, three shapes

notice.ask: *scrīpsit* and *audīvit* are different verbs. What do the two have in common?
notice.answer: Both say something already done, built on the third dictionary form
options: Both say something already done, built on the third dictionary form
Both say something happening now, built on the second dictionary form
Both describe a noun, built on the fourth dictionary form

teach.say: A dictionary gives a Latin verb four forms: *vocō, vocāre, vocāvī, vocātum*. These are **the principal parts (the four dictionary forms that give a verb's present, perfect and participle stems)**. The same verb three times — *vocat* 'he calls', *vocāvit* 'he called', *vocātus* 'called' — is three different stems, each cut from one of those forms.

check.ask: Which word here is built on a different stem from *vocat*?

teach.title: Part two gives the present stem
teach.say: The second form is the infinitive (the plain 'to' form), *vocāre*. Cut off its *-re* and you have the present stem, *vocā-*. Everything happening now, or going on, is built there and nowhere else: *vocat*, *scrībunt*, *mittit*. Parts three and four have nothing to do with these words.

check.ask: From the infinitive alone, fill in the 'he / she / it' form of the present.

teach.title: Part three gives the perfect stem: cut the -ī
teach.say: The third form is already a whole word — *vocāvī*, 'I called'. Cut its *-ī* and you have the perfect stem, *vocāv-*. Every 'did / has done' form of the verb is built on it: *vocāvit*, *scrīpsit*, *habuit*, *audīvit*. This is the part that surprises you, so it is the part to learn.

check.ask: Cut the -ī off the third part and add -it: fill in the cell.

teach.title: Part four gives the participle stem: cut the -um
teach.say: The fourth form ends in *-um*: *vocātum*. Cut that *-um* and you have the participle stem, *vocāt-*. From it comes the word for what was done to somebody — *vocātus*, *scrīpta*, *occīsa* — and the two-word past that uses it.

check.ask: Cut the -um off the fourth part and add -us: fill in the cell.

teach.title: Which part was this word cut from?
teach.say: Now the sorting. Three habits cover most verbs: *ā*-verbs are safe (*parāre, parāvī, parātum*); *ē*-verbs mostly go *-uī, -itum* (*habēre, habuī, habitum*); consonant verbs must be learned one at a time (*dūcere, dūxī, ductum*; *cadere, cecidī, cāsum*; *ferre, tulī, lātum*). When a form surprises you, ask which of the four it was cut from.

check.ask: *ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum*. Put 'he carried' in the gap.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) say the three stems are what matters, and that most verbs are predictable: ā-verbs go -āv-, -āt- (*laudāre, laudāv-, laudāt-*); ē-verbs mostly -u-, -it- (*monēre, monu-, monit-*); ī-verbs -īv-, -īt- (*audīre, audīv-, audīt-*). Consonant-stem verbs must be learned one by one: *scrībere, scrīps-, scrīpt-*; *dūcere, dūx-, duct-*; *dīligere, dīlēx-, dīlēct-*.

A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) has no perfect-active stem, so it shows only two parts plus the participle: *loquī, locūtum*; *lābī, lāpsum*. Ørberg lists new verbs at the foot of each chapter exactly this way: *pellere pepulisse pulsum*.
